vignette:
He is 29, European, single, and works in sales, a job that once fit his easy confidence. Before the disaster, he spends most days driving between clients, remembering names, reading a room quickly, and turning small talk into trust. He likes the rhythm of it: coffee on the go, polished shoes, a phone full of contacts, the sense that if he keeps moving and talking, life stays manageable.

The turning point comes during a severe flood that hits his town with little warning. He has finished a late client meeting and is driving home in heavy rain, annoyed more than worried, when the roads begin disappearing under brown water. At first he tells himself it will pass. He takes a detour, then another, but the water rises faster than he expects. His car stalls near an underpass, and within minutes the water is pressing against the doors. He remembers the strange silence inside the car between bursts of rain, the way his own breathing suddenly sounds too loud. When water starts spilling in around his ankles, panic takes over. He forces the door open against the pressure and climbs out into water strong enough to pull at his legs. He loses one shoe. His phone slips from his hand and vanishes. He grabs a road sign and holds on while debris knocks against him in the dark.

He can still picture a family in another car farther down, headlights half-submerged, a child crying somewhere he cannot see. He wants to move toward them but cannot keep his footing even where he is. He shouts, but his voice is swallowed by wind and water. Later he learns they were rescued. In his memory, though, they remain trapped in that moment, and so does he. Emergency crews eventually reach him by boat. By then he is shivering uncontrollably, embarrassed by how hard he clings to the rescuer's arm.

In the first days afterward, he tells the story like anyone would after a close call, with nervous laughter and a rehearsed punch line about ruining an expensive suit. Friends call him lucky. He agrees. He goes back to work quickly, partly because sales is unforgiving when he falls behind, partly because he wants proof that things are normal. But normal does not return.

Rain becomes the first problem. Even a steady shower on the windshield makes his chest tighten. He starts leaving absurdly early for appointments so he can avoid underpasses and roads near the river. If clouds gather, he cancels calls and invents excuses for clients. He checks weather apps over and over, as if vigilance might prevent another catastrophe. On good days he knows this is excessive; on bad days it feels like the only rational thing to do.

Sleep changes too. He wakes around 3 a.m. with his heart racing, sheets damp, convinced for a few seconds that water is rising in his room. Sometimes he dreams of being back in the car, unable to force the door open. Other nights the dream shifts and he hears the unseen child crying. He dreads going back to sleep once he wakes, so he scrolls on his phone or turns on the television for noise. By morning he feels wrung out and brittle.

At work, the effects show in ways that unsettle him. He misses details in conversations and has to ask clients to repeat themselves. During presentations, if he hears heavy rain against the building, his mind leaves the room. He watches windows, parking lots, drains. Once, during a storm, he abruptly ends a meeting and tells the client there is an emergency. Driving used to feel effortless; now he grips the wheel hard enough to leave his hands aching. He avoids entire sections of town, which makes his territory harder to cover and his numbers slip. His manager comments that he seems distracted. He laughs it off, then spends the rest of the day ashamed and angry with himself.

He is more irritable than he used to be. Friends notice he declines invitations if the forecast is poor, and even in good weather he often prefers to stay in his apartment, where he feels he has some control. He keeps a flashlight, bottled water, portable charger, and folded clothes by the door. He tells himself this is just preparedness, but he knows it is more than that. He scans exits in restaurants. He notices drains, gutters, river levels, the slope of streets. His world has reorganized around threat.

What troubles him most is not only the fear but the sense that the disaster has made him smaller. He used to think of himself as adaptable, the kind of person who could talk his way through anything. Now he feels hijacked by his own body. When rain starts, his thoughts narrow, his stomach clenches, and he is back at that underpass before he can tell himself he is safe. He does not talk much about the family in the other car, but when he does, his voice changes. He says he knows, logically, they survived. Still, part of him remains gripping that road sign in the dark, listening to water and feeling that terrible helplessness, as if the worst thing has not fully ended but is always about to begin again.
